lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on the future of war
lead.head: Swords, shields and software
body: When Amit Varma proposed an episode on the history of war, Ajay Shah replied “future of war”, again and again, until Varma saw he had a different idea. {#history}

Shah’s case was that much of what militaries know is already out of date. Wars from 1967 to the Gulf War, he said, were still recognisable by the standards of the Second World War. The last five years are not.
“The world has changed below our feet,” he said.
Why study war at all? Early states, Shah said, really did only one thing, wage war, and abhorring violence does not make war go away.

Military history moves in jumps. Aircraft carriers caught the Royal Navy off balance, and German tanks with Stuka dive bombers stunned Poland and France. Behind such jumps, he said, lies an endless dance between the sword and the shield. {112-C02}
## Six hard stories

Shah grounded his argument in six stories. Ukraine, with no navy to speak of, drove Russia’s fleet from the Black Sea. Ukrainian drones, assembled in secret inside Russia, flew out of trucks to strike five air bases. Mossad did much the same inside Iran.
On the Ukrainian front, two exhausted armies face each other across a no man’s land up to 30 kilometres deep, where drones see anything that moves.
## Nine principles

From the stories came nine principles. The first is that surprise and mass are gone: thanks to satellites, drones and open-source intelligence, every important campaign of the Russia-Ukraine war has been fully known to the other side. {112-C04}
Another is an inversion. At short range, defence now dominates. At long range, attack does: Ukrainian drones fly 1,000 to 2,000 kilometres into Russia and destroy factories night after night.
“It is very easy to kill a factory,” Shah said. “It is very difficult to win a trench.” {112-C06}

Equipment, he argued, has boiled down to something that moves, something that sees and something that kills. “The rest is all software.” A new revision pushed over the air becomes an instant upgrade for the whole force. {112-C08}
## The upshot

Conventional war, Shah said, is back despite nuclear weapons. Soldiers must be problem solvers, not merely brave. Factories must be able to surge in wartime, and procurement should buy civilian technology and move at the speed of Silicon Valley.
Above all, all roads lead to scale. Only the United States and China can reach it alone; everyone else, India included, must build with partners.

Varma, speaking as a layperson, ended with two fears. Wars will move at bewildering speed, tempting both sides to hand decisions to AI. And a country may not know whether it is at war at all, or with whom.
His hope was trade. “War helps no one, it’s a terrible negative sum game,” he said.
Shah agreed, while insisting that there is evil in the world and the state must be able to deal with it.
Varma’s farewell was four words: “Make trade, not war.”

second.label: The Ukraine front
second.head: One drone, one soldier
second.deck: Ajay Shah on a battlefield unlike any before it in world history
body: Two exhausted armies face each other in Ukraine across a battlefield like none other in world history, Ajay Shah said. In the First World War, trenches sat one or two kilometres apart. Here, no man’s land is 10, 20, 30 kilometres deep. {#nomansland}

Drones from both sides watch it constantly. Mass five hundred men and fifty tanks for an attack and they will be seen, and precision-guided munitions will destroy them. Russia, nearly out of Soviet equipment, has resorted to golf carts. {#golfcarts}

So soldiers huddle and hide, managing only small, dinky actions day after day. “They will send one drone to kill one soldier,” Shah said. {112-S06} Amit Varma noted that technology had expanded the hellscape, and it could grow further.

quote.text: This is the first time in world history that you have cruel, unrelenting drone coverage and precision guided munitions.

second.caption: the hellscape of the Ukraine front

third.head: Sand in the works
body: In the 1973 Yom Kippur War, Ajay Shah said, Israeli equipment in the Sinai desert stopped working properly. Tank treads and tyres were affected, and he thought some bridging equipment too, because the sand had characteristics nobody had seen before.
Then scientists “from the Weizmann Institute in Jerusalem came, sat there on the sand, did experiments with the sand, all while the war was going on”. {112-S11}
They went home and redesigned the bridging gear, and that, Shah said, is how Israel won the Sinai. Amit Varma’s verdict: “Human software.”

Modern war, Shah argued, is a game of more intelligence, so the military needs “wimps like Vaishnav”. Varma rose to his friend’s defence; Shah clarified that he meant “Vaishnav levels of genius”. {112-J13}
third.caption: the strange sand of the Sinai

p2.title: Tomorrow’s battlefield
p2.deck: Why war matters, what has changed, what India should do, and what Amit Varma fears

sections.label: Why war matters
sections.head: Peace was the easy part
sections.caption: why a pacifist must still study war
body: Why does a man who has railed against machismo care so much about war? Amit Varma put the question to Ajay Shah, who is invited to give talks to rooms full of generals.

Early states, Shah answered, really did only one thing: they waged war. Creating peace at home was not that hard or that expensive; by about 1900 the UK had figured out criminal justice. The frontier was war.
War forced states to build fiscal systems to raise money and to learn public procurement. It has driven scientific innovation again and again, and it shaped the very boundaries of states.
So disliking violence is not enough. “A simple insistence on pacifism does not solve the problem of war,” he said. {112-C01}
## Jumps, not steps

Force design has been thrown off balance again and again by new technology, Shah said. Attack and defence take turns: “Sometimes development in the techniques of war favour the sword. So attackers get an upper hand. Sometimes they favour the shield.” {112-C02}
People joke, he said, that Israel’s army in 1967 was Second World War capability fully realised. The Gulf War was “the first triumph of silicon over steel”. Both were recognisable. {112-J20}
Shah set the episode’s limits: no nuclear war, no insurgencies, just “simple mainline conventional war with a peer opponent”.
~ The lesson, he said, is never to fight the last war but always to look forward.

quote.text: A simple abhorrence of cruelty and violence doesn’t put an end to war.

sections.label: Probability one
sections.head: A sky full of drones
sections.caption: drone swarms, lasers and 3D printers
body: Ajay Shah named three technologies that are not yet used at scale but, he said, are coming “with probability one”.
The first is drone swarms: ten drones on one mission, talking to each other, then a hundred, a thousand, 10,000, swarms he expects to be “maddeningly large”. {#swarm}
Amit Varma greeted the escalation with a sporting metaphor. {112-J09}
Shah asked listeners to picture 6 June 1944, when people in Normandy were woken around 3 am by Allied planes flying from Britain for hours. That is the scene ahead, he said, except with drones.
## Light against the swarm
The second is Iron Beam, an Israeli system that fires lasers at drones. Imagine ten beams each killing ten drones a minute, Shah said, and 10,000 drones are not so scary. {#ironbeam}
The third is less glamorous: 3D printers carried close to the front to print spare parts for equipment that is forever breaking down.
Their friend Ayush Patnaik, Shah said, has built a 3D printer that prints everything about itself except one nozzle. Buy the nozzle, give Ayush a milkshake, and he will print you one. {112-J10}
~ Varma imagined aliens landing on Earth to find 3D printers the dominant species, with humans reduced to fossils.

quote.text: You just change the kitty party into a cricket match.

sections.label: The principles
sections.head: No surprises, no safe rear
sections.caption: nine principles for the new battlefield
body: Asked how he would revamp the military for the country’s grand leader, “a fellow Gujarati”, Ajay Shah began with principles, not actions. Great countries, he said, are not built out of getting shit done. {112-C03}
Logistics has become far harder. The enemy can see your ammunition dumps and supply trucks, and “a logistics truck is even more important than a tank”. {#truck}

Strategic wars are wars of economies, and the intelligence revolution has made them hungrier. Israel’s military fuses all its sensors into one targeting system, so targets per day, and the burn rate of munitions, have soared.
## The soldier as sensor
Some days, Shah said, a modern soldier is not so much fighting as form filling, reporting his position, his shells and the tank he thinks he sees. {112-C07}
That data lets an “Uber for artillery” match a target to the best-placed gun. Too much of it brings death by data, which he called the algorithmic fog of war.

His ninth and last principle was the pace of change. From September 1939 to Hiroshima, dogma was overturned every few months, and he believes this is such a moment again: “staying in the old ways is a certainty of doing badly”. {112-C10}
~ Amit Varma called it a masterclass and urged listeners to decide which principles they disagree with.

quote.text: As much as sending bullets out, the soldier is bringing information back. And information is power.

sections.label: What India should do
sections.head: Small, cheap and many
sections.caption: what India should build, and how
body: Nuclear weapons, Ajay Shah said, have not made conventional war obsolete. “No, conventional war is back.” {112-C12}
Amit Varma added that two guests on *The Seen and the Unseen* had made the counterintuitive case that nuclear weapons make conventional war more important, not less.
War now burns munitions faster than any peacetime factory supplies, so Shah wants surge capacity designed in: contracts for 100 tubes with the right, but not the obligation, to take 300. {#tubes}
## Off the shelf

Buy civilian technology wherever possible, he said. Starlink, a high-volume product, has immense military value. If shore-based missiles on Great Nicobar could dominate the Straits of Malacca, do you need aircraft carriers there?
Procurement, he said, must swap vendors like Raytheon and McDonnell Douglas and 30-year cycles for something closer to Silicon Valley. {112-C13}
Every sensible country, he said, should send teams to Ukraine, today’s equivalent of the Spanish Civil War, where Hitler perfected the Blitzkrieg. {112-C11}
Defence economics, Shah said, comes down to scale: only the United States and China can reach it alone, so everyone else must share gear with five to ten other countries. {112-C14}
~ India, Shah suggested, could make weapons for a Poland-Ukraine-South Korea partnership, since a factory in Tamil Nadu is far from any front.

quote.text: So we need to build surge capabilities into ordinary peacetime defence procurement, rather than running around when a war comes.

sections.label: Two fears, one hope
sections.head: The last human decision
sections.caption: two fears and one exhortation
body: Amit Varma came with two fears and one hope. The first fear began with Vasili Arkhipov, the Soviet submarine officer who refused to fire a nuclear torpedo in 1962.
Future wars, Varma said, will move at bewildering speed, and every side will be tempted to hand decisions to AI. Mistakes at that scale could be catastrophic. {112-C16}

His second fear was a new fog of war. A power cut, a GST or Aadhaar backend failure, contaminated water: is it an accident, terrorism or war? And is the culprit Pakistan, China, a dissident group, or the state in a false flag? {112-C17}
## Citizens, not subjects

Against them he set one hope: trade. Humanity has flourished through trade and peaceful cooperation, never war, he said; India should trade with China and Pakistan, and musicians on both sides should keep jamming. {112-C18}
His exhortation was to act as citizens: demand a state ready for future war, but one that actively makes peace with its neighbours.

Ajay Shah agreed, adding that there is evil in the world. He suggested doing for conventional war what Johnny von Neumann, John Nash and Thomas Schelling did for nuclear weapons after 1945: doctrines that produce more peace.
~ Varma hoped none of their worst fears come true, and that we trade until we can trade no more. {112-J16}

quote.text: What if the last human decision in a war is a decision to start the war?

side.boxText: Amit Varma had wanted a history-of-war episode built on *Conflict* by David Petraeus and Andrew Roberts, a book on the recent evolution of warfare that he enjoyed a few months ago. Ajay Shah steered them to the future. {112-R01}

contQuote.text: But if you actually look at the wider flourishing of humanity, the wider flourishing of humanity has never happened through war, it has always happened through trade, through peaceful cooperation

p3.title: War stories
p3.deck: Drones from trucks, boats that fire back, and one officer’s calm veto

stories.start: Operation Spider Web. Okay, just one of the world's great stories.
stories.end: And this will go down in history. This was Operation Spider Web.
stories.caption: Operation Spider Web
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the Ukrainian raid that began inside Russia
stories.head: Russia caught in a Spider Web
body: Over 18 months, Ajay Shah said, Ukrainian special forces shipped equipment and materials into safe houses inside Russia. One, they enjoyed pointing out, was in a building right next to an FSB office.
There they set up 3D printers, gathered parts and explosives and assembled 117 attack drones. Nothing was shipped in ready-made. {#attack-drones}

The drones were hidden in shipping containers on trucks. Each driver was an ordinary commercial driver, told some story and sent to wait at a pin on Google Maps, five to ten kilometres from one of five air bases: outside the fence, on civilian roads where nobody fusses over a parked truck.
By the time the trucks moved, not a single Ukrainian was left in Russia. Someone in Ukraine pressed a button, the roofs of the containers opened, and the drones flew out.
They rode ordinary data SIMs on the Russian mobile network, and some video is believed to have streamed over Telegram. They may even have carried onboard AI and a table of Russia’s costliest planes.

About twenty planes, central to the nightly bombing of Ukraine and worth perhaps two or three billion dollars, are believed to have been destroyed by drones costing about half a million dollars. {#halfmillion}
Zelensky announced that the operation had been 18 months in the making. “And that just makes you think what else are they working on?” Shah said. {112-S07}
~ Amit Varma added his favourite detail: the containers had false ceilings, so a cop who opened one would find nothing.
stories.why: Commercial off-the-shelf parts, a mobile data SIM and patience let a weaker country hit planes deep inside a stronger one. For Shah, a country’s interior is no longer safe, and every military planner should be thinking about such threats.
stories.postscript: Shah’s test for listeners: a genuine military geek knows the names of all the operations. This one, he said, will go down in history. {112-J06}

stories.start: I start at the contest for the Black Sea between Ukraine and Russia.
stories.end: Isn't it amazing? This is story number one.
stories.caption: the battle for the Black Sea
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on how a country with no navy won at sea
stories.head: Who needs a navy?
body: Early in the war, Ajay Shah believes, Ukraine’s navy was a single ship, which it scuttled so that the Russians could not capture it. {#nonavy}

Russia’s fleet sat in Sevastopol. Ukraine answered with three innovations. Drones and NATO-quality intelligence tracked every Russian ship in real time; shore-based missiles skimming two metres above the waves sank the Moskva; and drone boats carried a thousand kg of explosive. When Russian helicopters hunted the boats, they were redesigned to fire anti-air missiles back.

Russia stopped using Sevastopol, and Ukrainian commercial ships ply the Black Sea again. Shah credited a culture of engineering under fire: “I want to get an innovation out in the field next week.” {112-S05}
~ Shah relished the image of an arrogant helicopter, “the god of the sky”, shot down by a dumb boat. {112-J04}
stories.why: Amit Varma saw incentives at work: at a breakfast of bacon and eggs, the chicken is interested but the pig is committed, “and in that sense, Ukraine is a pig.” As his riddle went, the hare runs for his life. {112-J03}

stories.start: Gentle reader, you must remember all these names. Operation Rising Lion.
stories.end: which is called Iron Beam, and I will describe that as we go
stories.caption: Operation Rising Lion
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on Israel’s drones from inside Iran
stories.head: The lion that rose from within
body: Mossad operatives, Ajay Shah said, built a safe house inside Iran, shipped parts to themselves and used 3D printers to build large numbers of drones. Nobody yet knows how many.
In a synchronised assault, the drones took off inside Iran and knocked out a great deal of its air defences. Then Israeli planes arrived and hit targets all over the country.

Whether the nuclear programme was stopped is unknown; perhaps 400 kilograms of 60 per cent enriched uranium is still sitting around in Iran. {#uranium} But Iran’s conventional power, Shah said, was set back five or ten years. Iran hit back with probably 1,000 missiles and drones; about fifty, it is estimated, got through. {#fifty}
~ Shah called it a fascinating story of combining long-range action from Israel with covert operations inside Iran.

quote.text: So Israeli air defence is so great that essentially everything got killed in the sky.

stories.postscript: Amit Varma had a quiz: if the 1970s actor Ajit took part in an uprising, what would it be called? Operation Rising Loin. {112-J08}

stories.start: Have you heard of Vasily Arkhipov? So let me take you to October
stories.end: because one man was able to sit down and take a calm decision.
stories.caption: Vasili Arkhipov’s veto
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a Soviet officer’s veto in 1962
stories.head: The man who said ‘hold on’
body: In October 1962, Amit Varma said, during the Cuban Missile Crisis, a Soviet submarine called the B-59 was in the waters off Cuba, carrying nuclear torpedoes. At one point it came under attack.
Its captain thought the two countries were at war and that it was time to fire. But a launch needed three sign-offs: the captain, the political officer and the first officer.
The first officer, effectively second in command, was Vasili Arkhipov. Hold on, he said: if we are wrong, a nuclear first strike could set off a world war. He exercised his veto. {112-S12}
~ The torpedo was not fired, Varma said, “because one man was able to sit down and take a calm decision”.
stories.why: Process, and one calm person, kept a nuclear torpedo unfired. Varma told the story to frame his first fear: that wars fought at machine speed will tempt both sides to leave no room for such a pause. {112-C16}

quiz.q: Where did Indian and Pakistani planes stay while firing at each other, according to Ajay Shah?
quiz.a: High over their own territory, firing standoff weapons beyond visual range.

quiz.q: How quickly did Ukraine want new ideas on the battlefield, in Ajay Shah’s telling?
quiz.a: Next week: not lessons for a future war, but innovations in this one.

quiz.q: Who came to the Sinai battlefield in 1973 to experiment with its strange sand?
quiz.a: Scientists from the Weizmann Institute, who went home and redesigned the bridging gear.

quiz.q: What did Ajay Shah’s IIT wingmate Ajay Bhagavat say makes manufacturing harder than services?
quiz.a: Operating margins rarely top 15 per cent, leaving little cash to pay for learning.

quiz.q: Where, according to Ajay Shah, did Adolf Hitler perfect the Blitzkrieg?
quiz.a: In the Spanish Civil War of 1936, the lab of its day.

quiz.q: In Amit Varma’s riddle, who runs faster, the fox or the hare, and why?
quiz.a: The hare: the fox runs only for his lunch, the hare for his life.
